learn.hook: Every rupee the government spends, from building AIIMS hospitals to buying fighter jets, must first be approved by Parliament. No vote, no money.
points: The legislature is the central forum of representative democracy: it makes laws, debates public issues, and holds the executive accountable.

Functions of Parliament: legislative (law-making), control of the executive, financial (approving taxes and spending), representative, debating, constituent (amending the Constitution), electoral (electing the President and Vice-President) and judicial (impeachment and removal of judges).
Parliament represents the divergent views of members from different regions, social groups and parties, making it the most representative organ.
Many observers note a decline of legislatures relative to the executive: strong cabinets, party discipline and less time for debate shift power towards the government.
Even so, the legislature remains the only place where every law and every rupee must be openly justified to the people's representatives.

example.q: Classify each act of Parliament: (a) passing the Budget; (b) impeaching the President; (c) amending the Constitution; (d) electing the Vice-President.
steps: (a) Approving taxes and spending → financial function.
(b) Removing the head of state for violation of the Constitution → judicial function.
(c) Changing the Constitution → constituent function.
(d) Choosing the Vice-President → electoral function.

topics.title: Two Houses: Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha

learn.hook: Uttar Pradesh sends 31 members to the Rajya Sabha, Sikkim sends 1. In the US Senate, California and Wyoming send 2 each. Which is fairer?
points: Bicameral legislature: two Houses. India's Parliament has the Rajya Sabha (Council of States) and the Lok Sabha (House of the People). Most States have a unicameral legislature; a few (e.g. Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh) also have a Legislative Council.

Rajya Sabha represents the States. Its members are elected indirectly by the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (STV). It is a permanent House: never dissolved; members have six-year terms and one-third retire every two years.
Representation in the Rajya Sabha is based on population, so larger States get more seats (unequal representation), unlike the USA where every state has two Senators (equal representation).
The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha from among persons with special knowledge or experience in literature, science, art and social service.

Lok Sabha: directly elected by the people from territorial constituencies (543 seats), using FPTP; normal term five years, but it can be dissolved earlier if no government can be formed or on the PM's advice.

example.q: A Rajya Sabha member's term began in April 2020. When will it end, and why are RS elections held every two years?
steps: Each member's term is six years: April 2020 + 6 = April 2026.
One-third of members retire every two years, so elections are staggered.
Thus the House as a whole is never dissolved.
example.answer: April 2026; staggered retirement keeps the Rajya Sabha permanent.

learn.hook: The Rajya Sabha can debate the Budget for days — but it can't stop it. After 14 days, a money bill goes through anyway.
points: Exclusive powers of the Lok Sabha: money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; it approves the Budget; it alone can pass a no-confidence motion and remove the Council of Ministers.

Money bills: the Rajya Sabha can only discuss a money bill and suggest changes within 14 days; the Lok Sabha may accept or reject these suggestions. The Speaker decides whether a bill is a money bill.
On ordinary (non-money) bills, both Houses have equal powers; if they disagree, a joint sitting can be called.

Special powers of the Rajya Sabha: under Article 249 it can authorise Parliament, by a two-thirds resolution, to make laws on a State List subject in the national interest; it can also authorise the creation of new All India Services.
Overall, the Lok Sabha is more powerful because it represents the people directly and controls money and the ministry.

example.q: The Lok Sabha passes a money bill on 1 March and sends it to the Rajya Sabha. The Rajya Sabha does nothing. What happens?
steps: The Rajya Sabha must return a money bill with recommendations within 14 days.
If it does not return it within 14 days, the bill is deemed passed by both Houses.
So after 15 March the bill is deemed passed in the form passed by the Lok Sabha.
example.answer: The bill is deemed passed by both Houses after 14 days.

learn.hook: A bill is like a train leaving a station: it must stop at several junctions — readings, committees, the other House, and Rashtrapati Bhavan — before it reaches its destination as an Act.
points: A bill is a draft of a proposed law. Government bills are introduced by ministers; private members' bills are introduced by MPs who are not ministers.
Money bills deal with taxes, borrowing and spending; they can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. Non-money (ordinary) bills can be introduced in either House.

Stages: drafting by the ministry → introduction (first reading) → referral to a committee for detailed study → second reading (detailed, clause-by-clause consideration) → third reading (vote on the bill as a whole).
The bill then goes to the other House, which follows a similar process. If the Houses disagree on an ordinary bill, the President can summon a joint sitting, presided over by the Speaker.
Finally, the bill goes to the President for assent; once assent is given, the bill becomes an Act (law).

example.q: Arrange the life of a government bill on road safety from idea to law.
steps: The ministry drafts the bill after consultations.
A minister introduces it in a House (first reading).
It is referred to a committee, then debated clause by clause (second reading).
It is voted on (third reading), then passed by the other House.
The President gives assent and it becomes an Act.
example.answer: Draft → introduce → committee → clause-by-clause → vote → other House → assent → Act.

learn.reallife: Every new traffic fine, tax change or consumer protection rule you read about began as a bill that crossed each of these junctions before the President signed it.

learn.hook: The first hour of a Lok Sabha sitting belongs to MPs' questions. Ministers must answer — on rail accidents, prices, exam leaks, anything. It's called Question Hour.
points: Deliberation and discussion: Question Hour (MPs ask ministers questions), Zero Hour (members raise urgent matters, an Indian innovation), adjournment motions (to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance), half-hour discussions and calling attention motions.
Approval and ratification: a government needs Parliament to pass its laws and policies, giving Parliament leverage over the executive.
Financial control: Parliament approves the Budget and demands for grants; the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) audits government accounts, and the Public Accounts Committee examines CAG reports.
No-confidence motion: the ultimate weapon; if passed by the Lok Sabha, the government must resign.
Limits: a government with a strong majority and strict party discipline may face weaker parliamentary control; frequent disruptions also reduce debate time.

example.q: Match each situation to a tool: (a) MP wants the Railway Minister's answer on delays; (b) MPs want to set aside normal business to discuss a sudden flood; (c) the Opposition wants the government removed.
steps: (a) Asking a minister a question → Question Hour.
(b) Urgent matter needing discussion → adjournment motion.
(c) Removing the government → no-confidence motion.
example.answer: (a) Question Hour, (b) adjournment motion, (c) no-confidence motion.

quiz.explain: Passing it forces the entire government to resign.

Lesson: the no-confidence motion – if passed, the government must resign.
Answer: No-confidence motion

quiz.q: Who audits the accounts of the Union government and reports to Parliament?
quiz.explain: The CAG audits government spending; reports go to Parliament.
steps: Asked: who audits Union government accounts.
Lesson: the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG).
Answer: The Comptroller and Auditor General

quiz.q: The Public Accounts Committee examines
options: the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General
quiz.explain: The PAC scrutinises CAG audit reports.
steps: Asked: what the Public Accounts Committee examines.
Lesson: the PAC examines CAG reports.
Answer: the reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General

quiz.q: What is Zero Hour?
options: Time when members raise urgent issues, an Indian parliamentary innovation
The time when no business is transacted
The time reserved for the President's address
quiz.explain: Zero Hour follows Question Hour and allows urgent matters to be raised.
steps: Asked: what Zero Hour is.
Lesson: members raise urgent matters; it is an Indian innovation.
Answer: Time when members raise urgent issues, an Indian parliamentary innovation

quiz.q: Why may parliamentary control over the executive be weak when the ruling party has a large majority?
options: Party discipline ensures government bills and motions pass easily
The President takes over the ministry
quiz.explain: Large majorities plus discipline reduce effective control.
steps: Asked: why control weakens with a large majority.
Lesson: a strong majority with strict party discipline faces weaker control.
Government business passes easily.
Answer: Party discipline ensures government bills and motions pass easily
quiz.mistake: Invents constitutional changes

quiz.q: Assertion (A): An adjournment motion is a means of parliamentary control. Reason (R): It allows the House to set aside its normal business to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; discussing urgent failures of government is how it acts as control.
steps: A: an adjournment motion is a means of control – true.
R: it sets aside normal business to discuss an urgent public matter – true.
Discussing urgent matters is how it controls, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: A government needs Parliament to pass its bills and its budget. This gives Parliament control through
quiz.explain: Without Parliament's approval, the executive's plans cannot become law.
steps: Given: the government needs Parliament to pass its bills and budget.
Lesson: this is control through approval and ratification.
Answer: approval and ratification
quiz.mistake: Picks a judicial or presidential power

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'Once a government is formed, can it do anything it wants until the next election?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Questions, motions, money control and the no-confidence motion. The government is always on its toes!
teach.nudge: What can MPs do if they want to remove a government?

revise.summary: Parliament controls the executive through Question Hour, Zero Hour and motions, by approving laws and money, through CAG audits and the PAC, and ultimately the no-confidence motion.

Adjournment motion: discuss a definite urgent public matter
PAC examines CAG reports; no-confidence motion forces resignation

The CAG audits; the PAC examines CAG reports

topics.title: Committees and how Parliament regulates itself

learn.hook: A 300-page bill on data protection cannot be studied properly in a noisy House of 543. So Parliament sends it to a small committee of MPs from many parties who meet quietly, call experts and go clause by clause.
points: Standing committees are permanent; department-related standing committees scrutinise bills, demands for grants and the working of ministries. Ad hoc committees are set up for a specific purpose and end when their task is over.
Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPC) have members from both Houses and may be set up to examine a bill or investigate financial irregularities.
Committees allow detailed, less partisan study, and their reports guide the House.

The presiding officer (Speaker in the Lok Sabha, Chairman in the Rajya Sabha) is the final authority on conduct of business in the House. Members enjoy parliamentary privileges, e.g. no court action for anything said in the House.

Anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985; Tenth Schedule): a member elected on a party ticket who leaves the party or defies the party whip can be disqualified; the presiding officer decides. The 91st Amendment (2003) tightened it by removing the 'split' exception.

example.q: An MP elected on Party X's ticket votes against the party's whip in a crucial vote without permission. What can follow?
steps: Defying the party whip without permission is ground for disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
The party can petition the presiding officer.
The Speaker or Chairman decides whether the member is disqualified.
example.answer: He can be disqualified under the anti-defection law, as decided by the presiding officer.

learn.reallife: Bills on data protection, forests and criminal law have been sent to Joint or Standing Committees, where MPs from rival parties sit around one table and invite experts and citizens' groups.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of parliamentary committees?
options: They allow detailed, expert and less partisan scrutiny of bills and government work
They replace the need for elections
They make laws without the House's approval
quiz.explain: Committees study matters in depth on behalf of the House.
steps: Asked: main advantage of committees.
Lesson: committees allow detailed, less partisan study; reports guide the House.
They do not replace elections or pass laws themselves.
Answer: They allow detailed, expert and less partisan scrutiny of bills and government work
quiz.mistake: Thinks committees have final law-making power

quiz.q: Which committee is set up with members of both Houses to examine a bill or investigate irregularities?
quiz.explain: JPCs include members of both Houses.
steps: Asked: committee with members of both Houses.
Lesson: Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPC).
Answer: Joint Parliamentary Committee
quiz.mistake: Confuses JPC with other committees

quiz.q: The anti-defection law was introduced by which amendment?
quiz.explain: The 52nd Amendment added the Tenth Schedule.

Lesson: the 52nd Amendment (1985) added the Tenth Schedule.
Answer: 52nd Amendment (1985)

quiz.q: Who decides whether a member is disqualified under the anti-defection law?

steps: Asked: who decides disqualification for defection.
Lesson: the presiding officer (Speaker/Chairman) decides.
Answer: The presiding officer of the House
quiz.mistake: Thinks the EC or party decides

quiz.q: A member of the Lok Sabha cannot be sued in court for a speech made in the House. This is an example of
quiz.explain: Freedom of speech in the House is a parliamentary privilege.

Lesson: this is a parliamentary privilege.
Answer: parliamentary privilege
quiz.mistake: Confuses privilege with other doctrines

quiz.q: What did the 91st Amendment (2003) change in the anti-defection law?
options: It removed the exception that protected a 'split' by one-third of a party's members
It allowed members to defect freely
It moved the decision to the Supreme Court
quiz.explain: After 2003, a split is no longer a defence; only a merger supported by two-thirds is protected.
steps: Asked: what the 91st Amendment changed.
Lesson: it tightened the law by removing the 'split' exception.
Answer: It removed the exception that protected a 'split' by one-third of a party's members
quiz.mistake: Thinks the amendment weakened the law

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Department-related standing committees improve the quality of legislation. Reason (R): They examine bills and ministries' work in detail and include members from different parties.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; detailed, cross-party scrutiny is why they improve laws.
steps: A: standing committees improve legislation – true.
R: they examine bills and ministries in detail with cross-party members – true.
That scrutiny is why laws improve, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see how committee features improve laws

quiz.q: Which officer is the final authority on the conduct of business in the Lok Sabha?
quiz.explain: The Speaker regulates proceedings and decides points of order.
steps: Asked: final authority on Lok Sabha business.
Lesson: the presiding officer – the Speaker in the Lok Sabha.
Answer: The Speaker
quiz.mistake: Thinks the PM controls the House's proceedings

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'How can a few MPs in a room help 543 others? And what stops MPs from hopping parties?'
teach.praise: Yay! Committees do the deep work, the Speaker runs the House, and the anti-defection law stops party-hopping!
teach.nudge: What happens to an MP who leaves his party after being elected?

revise.summary: Parliament works through standing, ad hoc and joint committees. Presiding officers run the House, members have privileges, and the Tenth Schedule disqualifies defectors, as decided by the presiding officer.
focus: Parliamentary privilege and the presiding officer's role
Anti-defection law and the 91st Amendment change
remember: JPC has members from both Houses
traps: Disqualification is decided by the presiding officer, not the Election Commission
Ad hoc committees end when their task is over; standing committees are permanent
